script.title: Unlocking the Secrets of Chemical Changes
script.subtitle: Master how substances transform, balance, and react in real-world scenarios.

steps.body: Look for color changes, gas evolution, or temperature shifts to spot a reaction.
Convert word equations into chemical formulas using correct symbols and states (s, l, g, aq).
Apply the Law of Conservation of Mass by ensuring atoms on reactant side equal product side.

script.example: Balance: Fe + H2O -> Fe3O4 + H2. Solution: 3Fe + 4H2O -> Fe3O4 + 4H2. Atoms: Fe(3=3), H(8=8), O(4=4).
script.ctaBody: Solve the NCERT in-text questions to test your balancing speed.
script.videoPrompt: A 3D molecular view of magnesium ribbon burning in oxygen to form white magnesium oxide powder.

topics.heading: Chemical Equations and Balancing
topics.explain: A chemical equation is a shorthand way to represent a reaction using symbols. It is like a recipe where the ingredients (reactants) must exactly equal the finished dish (products) to satisfy the Law of Conservation of Ma
bullets: Reactants are on the left, products on the right.
Use coefficients to balance, never change subscripts.
State symbols: (s) solid, (l) liquid, (g) gas, (aq) aqueous.
topics.visual: A digital scale balancing atoms of Hydrogen and Oxygen on both sides.

topics.heading: Combination and Decomposition Reactions
topics.explain: Combination is when two elements join to form one product, like two people hugging. Decomposition is the opposite, where one compound breaks into two or more parts, like a single Lego structure being pulled apart.
topics.visual: A single molecule splitting into two smaller fragments under a heat lamp.

topics.heading: Displacement and Double Displacement Reactions
topics.explain: In displacement, a stronger element kicks out a weaker one from its place, like a star player replacing a bench player. In double displacement, two compounds exchange partners to form new ones.
bullets: Double Displacement: AB + CD -> AD + CB
Often involves the formation of a precipitate (insoluble solid).
topics.visual: An iron nail turning brownish as copper ions are displaced from a blue solution.

topics.heading: Oxidation and Reduction (Redox)
topics.explain: Oxidation is the gain of oxygen or loss of electrons, while reduction is the loss of oxygen or gain of electrons. Think of it as a dance where one person gives a prop (oxygen) and the other receives it.
bullets: Oxidizing agent: The substance that gives oxygen.
Reducing agent: The substance that takes oxygen.
Redox occurs when both processes happen simultaneously.
topics.example: CuO + H2 -> Cu + H2O (CuO is reduced, H2 is oxidized).
topics.visual: Oxygen atoms moving from a copper oxide molecule to a hydrogen molecule.

topics.heading: Corrosion and Rancidity
topics.explain: Corrosion is the slow eating away of metals by air and moisture, like rust on an old gate. Rancidity is the oxidation of fats and oils in food, making them smell bad, similar to how an apple turns brown.
bullets: Prevent corrosion via galvanization or painting.
Prevent rancidity by using nitrogen gas in food packets.
topics.example: Silver turning black due to silver sulphide formation.
topics.visual: A shiny iron bolt slowly transforming into a crumbly orange-brown texture.

script.misconception: Students often change subscripts (e.g., changing H2O to H2O2) to balance equations. Never change subscripts; only change the coefficients in front of the formulas.
script.examTip: Always write the physical states (s, l, g, aq) in your final balanced equation to score full marks in long-answer questions.
sources: NCERT Class 10 Science: Chemical Reactions and Equations
